content:
Is there any existing work on absolutely monotone functions in mathlib or in progress?
(revised definition):

A function f : R -> R is absolutely monotone on a set s if it is smooth and all its iterated derivatives are nonneg on s. We have a formalization:

structure AbsolutelyMonotoneOn (f : ℝ → ℝ) (s : Set ℝ) : Prop where
  contDiff : ContDiff ℝ ⊤ f
  nonneg_iteratedDeriv : ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ x ∈ s, 0 ≤ iteratedDeriv n f x

We bundle ContDiff into the definition to avoid issues with junk values: without it, a nowhere-differentiable function would vacuously satisfy 0 ≤ iteratedDeriv n f x since mathlib's iteratedDeriv defaults to 0 at non-differentiable points.

What we have so far:

  • Closure under add, smul, mul
  • Examples: exp, cosh, pow, nonneg constants
  • Bernstein characterization (both directions): abs monotone on [0, ∞) iff power series with nonneg coefficients

The application is a generalized Schur exponential theorem: entrywise application of any function with a nonneg-coefficient power series preserves positive semidefiniteness, building on the Schur product theorem (#37297).

Questions:

  1. Is bundling ContDiff the right approach, or would a power-series-based definition be preferred?
  2. We use AbsolutelyMonotoneOn throughout (no unqualified AbsolutelyMonotone to avoid confusion with mathlib's convention that unqualified names mean Set.univ). Is this the right call?
  3. Placement: Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/AbsolutelyMonotone.lean?

On the ContDiff question: mathematically the definition should require smoothness only on s (ContDiffOn), but we use global ContDiff because mathlib's iteratedDeriv lemmas (iteratedDeriv_add, iteratedDeriv_mul, etc.) require global ContDiffAt, not ContDiffOn. Using iteratedDerivWithin + ContDiffOn would be more correct but significantly harder to work with. Happy to change if there's a preferred pattern for this.

Michael R Douglas said:

A function f : R -> R is absolutely monotone on a set s if it is smooth and

structure AbsolutelyMonotoneOn (f : ℝ → ℝ) (s : Set ℝ) : Prop where
  contDiff : ContDiff ℝ ⊤ f

I'm pretty sure that ContDiff ℝ ⊤ f means f is real-analytic

ok, we got it to work with

structure AbsolutelyMonotoneOn (f : ℝ → ℝ) (s : Set ℝ) : Prop where
    contDiffOn : ContDiffOn ℝ ⊤ f s
    nonneg : ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ x ∈ s, 0 ≤ iteratedDerivWithin n f s x
Doesn’t this still say that f is analytic, rather than that f is smooth? I think you should use ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ f s instead

Michael R Douglas said:

ok, we got it to work with

structure AbsolutelyMonotoneOn (f : ℝ → ℝ) (s : Set ℝ) : Prop where
    contDiffOn : ContDiffOn ℝ ⊤ f s
    nonneg : ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ x ∈ s, 0 ≤ iteratedDerivWithin n f s x

This already looked much nicer!
Btw, are your trials on some repo/PR? i would like to try an idea but it would be easier if I can compare it against your current experiments.
You should still only assume ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ f s (i.e., smooth and not analytic). You may need to open scoped ContDiff for this notation to be available.

Good point — yes, we've updated the definition to use ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ f s:

structure AbsolutelyMonotoneOn (f : ℝ → ℝ) (s : Set ℝ) : Prop where
  contDiffOn : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ f s
  nonneg : ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ x ∈ s, 0 ≤ iteratedDerivWithin n f s x

The closure properties, examples, and nonneg power series → abs monotone all go through with the smooth definition.

We are doing this for a downstream application — the generalized Schur exponential theorem that entrywise application of f to a PSD matrix is PSD — for which we need f to equal its Taylor series, not just have nonneg Taylor coefficients. Smoothness is not enough. Fortunately there is a theorem of Bernstein that smooth + nonneg iterated derivatives on a convex set containing 0 ⟹ analytic. This gives f(x) = Σ aₙ xⁿ with aₙ ≥ 0, which lets us write f(A) entrywise as Σ aₙ · A⊙ⁿ and apply Schur. We proved it:

theorem analyticWithinAt_zero_of_nonneg_iteratedDerivWithin {f : ℝ → ℝ} {s : Set ℝ}
    (hs : UniqueDiffOn ℝ s) (hconv : Convex ℝ s) (h0 : (0 : ℝ) ∈ s)
    (hf_smooth : ∀ n : ℕ, ContDiffOn ℝ n f s)
    (hf_nonneg : ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ x ∈ s, 0 ≤ iteratedDerivWithin n f s x)
    (hpos : ∃ y ∈ s, 0 < y) :
    AnalyticWithinAt ℝ f s 0

The proof uses Taylor's theorem with integral remainder + a Widder-style bound. It's about 500 lines. We use AnalyticWithinAt rather than AnalyticAt because the Taylor series only needs to agree with f on s.

We'll put together a draft PR with AbsolutelyMonotoneOn, Bernstein (both directions), and the PSD application (generalized Schur exponential), so you can see the full picture.

The assumption hf_smooth : ∀ n : ℕ, ContDiffOn ℝ n f s should instead be spellt hf_smooth : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ f s. Also, you can certainly drop the assumptions hs and hpos from your statement (and maybe also h0)

Draft PR is up: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/37879

Pushed the first change: theorem now takes ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ f s instead of ∀ n : ℕ, ContDiffOn ℝ n f s.

For dropping hs, hpos, h0 — could you clarify? A few cases:

  • hs : UniqueDiffOn ℝ s is used throughout the proof body for iteratedDerivWithin lemmas. Can be derived from Convex + nonempty interior, but we need nonempty interior from somewhere. With h0 and hpos, [0, y₀] ⊆ s has nonempty interior (0, y₀), so we could derive it.

  • hpos : ∃ y ∈ s, 0 < y provides the Widder witness for the proof strategy. Without it, if s = {0}, the conclusion AnalyticWithinAt ℝ f {0} 0 seems nontrivial to establish (would need p.sum 0 = f 0 for some formal power series).

  • h0 : 0 ∈ s — used to apply Taylor at 0.

Are you suggesting we derive hs from hconv + h0 + hpos internally? Or that there is a simpler proof path that avoids these hypotheses altogether? Would appreciate any hint.

There are two cases. If s = {0}, then the result is trivially true (there is essentially nothing to prove). Otherwise, there is a nonzero point in s, then s has nonempty interior, therefore you can derive hs.

The math question is whether it's important that the nonzero point in s is positive, or if a negative one would also be good enough.

On the math question: yes, we need a positive witness y₀ ∈ s. The Widder bound a_k · y₀^k ≤ f(y₀) relies on all terms of the partial sum being nonneg, which only works when y₀ > 0. Once we have it, convergence is automatic on (-y₀, y₀) ∩ s, so the positive witness also gives analyticity on the negative side (if s extends there). With only negative witnesses, the alternating signs break the Widder argument and a different proof path would be needed. I'll case-split and drop hs (derivable from convex + nonempty interior when s ≠ {0}), and ask the reviewer on the PR whether to require positive specifically or just nonzero.
@Sébastien Gouëzel, I simplified PR #38026, how does it look?

Thanks for merging! The content trimmed from #37879 is ready to come back as smaller focused PRs. Could you suggest a preferred ordering? Tentative stages:

  1. Examples — absolutelyMonotoneOn_exp, absolutelyMonotoneOn_cosh, absolutelyMonotoneOn_pow, absolutelyMonotoneOn_const. Each a few lines via of_contDiff; total ~60 lines.
  2. HasFTaylorSeriesUpToOn.mul — the Leibniz product rule you flagged on April 27 as a missing Mathlib lemma. Standalone, useful beyond AbsolutelyMonotone.
  3. AbsolutelyMonotoneOn.mul closure — returns the lemma deferred from this PR; depends on (2).
  4. Bernstein, backward direction — absolutelyMonotoneOn_of_nonneg_coeffs: a convergent power series with nonneg coefficients is absolutely monotone on Ici 0. ~150 lines, independent.
  5. Bernstein, forward direction — AbsolutelyMonotoneOn.analyticAt_zero: abs monotone with 0 ∈ s implies analytic at 0. ~500 lines; may itself need splitting (e.g., extracting a generic real-analysis lemma). Independent.
  6. Schur exponential application — entrywise application of an absolutely monotone function preserves positive semidefiniteness. Lives under Mathlib/Analysis/Matrix/. Depends on (4).

Independent groups: {1}, {2,3}, {4}, {5} can proceed in parallel; (6) needs (4).

There is an issue here that the main bottleneck for Mathlib growth is reviewer's time. Our strategy has been to do very careful reviews from which the PRs authors learn, and when they have learnt enough they can review PRs themselves -- giving a virtuous cycle that can lead to (exponential) growth. This doesn't happen when the PRs are mostly AI generated, so most reviewers have chosen not to devote time to AI generated PRs. My advice in this case is not to submit to Mathlib, but instead to build a project downstream of Mathlib in which you will not be limited by Mathlib's reviewer time.

I would like to point out that, although this has been our historical reviewing strategy, there is no evidence that it will stay that way much longer. We do want mathematicians like you who aren't necessarily incredibly proficient at Lean (because of lack of interest or time) to contribute efficiently to mathlib. But there is a problem to solve here first.
